---
title: Making yogurt at home
lang: en
free: true
---
Yogurt is a fermented dairy product created when specific bacterial cultures convert lactose into lactic acid. The acid denatures milk proteins, causing them to tangle into a gel that gives yogurt its characteristic thick, creamy texture. Unlike bread fermentation, no gas is produced; the transformation is purely biochemical and happens in a warm, undisturbed environment.

## Heating and inoculating the milk

Whole or reduced-fat milk is heated to 82–85 °C and held briefly to denature whey proteins—this step is what separates yogurt from simple curdled milk, producing a smoother final texture. The milk is then cooled to 43–46 °C before adding a starter: two to three tablespoons of live-culture plain yogurt or a freeze-dried starter sachet. The bacteria, primarily _Lactobacillus delbrueckii_ subsp. _bulgaricus_ and _Streptococcus thermophilus_, need this narrow temperature range to thrive.

## Incubation and thickening

The inoculated milk is poured into jars and kept at 43–46 °C for six to eight hours—inside an oven with only the light on, a yogurt maker, or wrapped in towels. Moving the jars during incubation breaks the forming gel. Once set, yogurt is refrigerated for at least two hours; acidity continues to develop slowly in the cold, firming the curd and sharpening the flavour.
